name: Peridot
physical: Traditionally associated with vitality and freshness
Said to bring a cleansed, lively feeling
Crystal healers link it with a sense of renewal
summary: Peridot is the lime-green gem of volcanic fire and meteorites, called the evening emerald and linked in crystal lore with renewal, joy and abundance.
intro: Peridot is the gem form of olivine, and it is one of the few gemstones that occurs in only one colour: a fresh, lively green that ranges from yellow-green to deep olive depending on its iron content. Crystals form deep in the Earth's mantle and are carried to the surface by volcanic eruptions, which is why peridot is found in lava and basalt on Hawaii and in Arizona. It has also been found in pallasite meteorites, as tiny green crystals in iron. Its colour glows warmly in lamplight, which is why it earned the nickname evening emerald. A good stone has a gentle, silky-looking sheen.
history: Peridot has been mined for more than three thousand years, notably on the Red Sea island of Zabargad, which was called Topazios by the Greeks and later St John's Island. Ancient Egyptians called it the gem of the sun and reportedly mined it at night, when its glow could be spotted on the ground. Many large green gems in medieval European churches were later found to be peridot, not emerald. The name probably comes from the Arabic faridat, meaning gem. Pallasite meteorites, including the Esquel meteorite from Argentina, have supplied space-born peridot. Today it is the August birthstone.
meaning: In crystal tradition peridot is a stone of renewal, abundance and emotional release. Practitioners say it helps clear out old resentments, jealousy and stagnation, making room for fresh growth. It is linked to the heart and solar plexus chakras, bridging love and personal power, and is used in rituals to attract prosperity and joy. Because it comes from deep in the Earth and sometimes from space, some healers treat it as a stone of cosmic perspective. Folk tradition says it protects against nightmares and brings good fortune to the wearer. Physically it is traditionally associated with vitality and freshness, as a supportive symbol and not a treatment.
howToUse: Wear peridot as a ring or pendant to encourage optimism and a generous outlook. Place a stone in your wallet or on your desk to support abundance intentions, or put three pieces in the wealth corner of your home. During meditation, hold a piece to the heart and breathe slowly, picturing a spring green meadow. Use it in a grid with citrine and green aventurine to attract prosperity. A small stone by your bed is traditionally said to ease restless thoughts.
care: Peridot is only moderately hard and can be brittle, so protect it from knocks and scratches. Clean it with lukewarm water and a soft cloth, and avoid ultrasonic cleaners, acids and steam, as it is sensitive to acid. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight. Extended strong sunlight and heat may affect its colour, so avoid leaving it on a sunny windowsill. Store separately in a soft pouch, away from harder gems like sapphire and diamond.
identify: Peridot has a recognisable olive to lime green colour and a slightly oily look, with strong double refraction that makes facet edges look doubled through the stone. Look-alikes include green tourmaline, moldavite, chrysoberyl, demantoid garnet, green sapphire and glass. Natural stones often show tiny lily-pad inclusions. Peridot is rarely treated, though cleaning may be done. Ask for origin information, and compare with a known sample if you suspect glass.

faq.a: In crystal tradition peridot is used for renewal, abundance and releasing envy or old resentment. It is linked with the heart and solar plexus chakras and is a popular stone for fresh starts.

faq.q: Is peridot the same as olivine?
faq.a: Peridot is the gem-quality form of olivine. Most olivine is a common rock-forming mineral that is not clear enough to cut, while peridot crystals are transparent and bright green.

faq.q: Is it true peridot comes from meteorites?
faq.a: Some does. Pallasite meteorites contain olivine crystals that can be cut as peridot. Most peridot, though, is mined from volcanic rocks and the Earth's upper mantle.
